title: What is S3, what are its storage classes (Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Standard-IA, One Zone-IA, Glacier Instant/Flexible/Deep Archive), and how do lifecycle policies transition or expire objects to save cost?
shortTitle: S3, Storage Classes, and Lifecycle Policies
keyPoints: S3 is highly durable object storage with eleven nines of durability, storing files as objects in buckets accessed over HTTP APIs.
S3 Standard is for frequently accessed data; Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between tiers based on real usage patterns.
Standard-IA and One Zone-IA are cheaper for infrequently accessed data, with One Zone-IA trading durability for lower cost by using a single Availability Zone.
Glacier classes provide archival storage: Instant Retrieval (milliseconds), Flexible Retrieval (minutes to hours), and Deep Archive (up to twelve hours).
Lifecycle policies transition objects to cheaper classes as they age and expire them when retention is met, all automatically.
Transitions have per-object charges and minimum storage durations, so moving millions of tiny objects too early can cost more than it saves.

s1_definition.oneliner: S3 stores files as objects with extreme durability, storage classes trade retrieval speed for cost, and lifecycle policies automatically move and delete objects as they age to cut the bill.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **S3 (Simple Storage Service)** – a highly durable, virtually unlimited object storage service that stores files as objects inside buckets, accessed over HTTP APIs, with eleven nines (99.999999999%) of durability.
- **Storage classes** – tiers tuned to different access patterns: Standard for frequent access, Intelligent-Tiering for unknown patterns, Standard-IA and One Zone-IA for infrequent access, and Glacier classes for archival.
- **Glacier tiers** – Instant Retrieval (milliseconds), Flexible Retrieval (minutes to hours), and Deep Archive (up to twelve hours retrieval).
- **Lifecycle policy** – a set of rules on a bucket that automatically transitions objects to cheaper classes as they age and expires (deletes) them when retention is met.
- **Cost model** – you pay for storage, requests, retrieval (for IA/Glacier classes), and data transfer out.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of S3 as the giant document warehouse of National Bank of India where every statement PDF, scanned cheque, and KYC document is stored. The storage classes are different shelves. The front shelf (Standard) is for this month's statements that customers open often – fast but expensive. A middle shelf (Standard-IA) is for last year's documents opened occasionally. A deep basement vault (Glacier Deep Archive) is for ten-year-old records the bank must legally keep but almost never opens – very cheap but slow to fetch. A lifecycle policy is the warehouse rule that says "after 30 days move a statement from the front shelf to the middle shelf, after one year to the basement, and after ten years shred it," done automatically.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Amazon S3 is highly durable object storage that keeps files as objects inside buckets, accessed over HTTP APIs, and gives eleven nines of durability by replicating data across multiple devices and Availability Zones. Unlike a disk, it is effectively unlimited, and you pay for what you store and retrieve.

The storage classes let you trade retrieval speed against cost based on how often data is accessed. S3 Standard is for frequently accessed data with low latency. Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves each object between frequent and infrequent tiers based on real usage, which is ideal when the access pattern is unknown. Standard-IA and One Zone-IA are cheaper for infrequently accessed data, with One Zone-IA trading durability for a lower price by living in a single Availability Zone. The Glacier classes are archival: Instant Retrieval returns in milliseconds, Flexible Retrieval in minutes to hours, and Deep Archive is the cheapest at up to twelve hours for long-term compliance data.

Lifecycle policies are what make this automatic and affordable. I attach rules to a bucket that transition objects to colder classes as they age and finally expire them when retention is met, and the rules can also clean up old versions and incomplete multipart uploads. The nuance I always raise is that transitions carry small per-object charges and minimum durations, so transitioning millions of tiny objects too aggressively can cost more than it saves, and for unpredictable access patterns Intelligent-Tiering is safer than a fixed-age rule because it reacts to actual usage.

At National Bank of India we generated millions of statement PDFs that are opened heavily in the first month, rarely after that, yet must be retained for ten years by regulation. I wrote a lifecycle policy that keeps new statements in Standard, moves them to Standard-IA after thirty days, to Glacier Flexible Retrieval after ninety days, to Deep Archive after a year, and expires them at ten years. That single policy cut our storage bill by over ninety percent while meeting the retention rule, and because it runs automatically no one ever has to move a file by hand.

Remember one sentence: S3 storage classes trade retrieval speed for cost, and lifecycle policies automate the transitions as data ages, so you pay the cheapest rate for each object based on how often it is actually accessed.
